          "text": "# Ankaa: A Phoenix Star with a Hidden Partner\n\n*One bright point in the southern sky is a giant star\u2014and, in its changing spectrum, a record of a companion circling out of sight.*\n\nOn a clear evening in the Southern Hemisphere, Ankaa offers a simple pleasure: a bright, steady point of light in a constellation that can otherwise be easy to overlook. SIMBAD classifies Ankaa as a spectroscopic binary: two stars orbit one another, though they are not ordinarily seen as a pair in the sky. Astronomers infer the companion by studying the light. As the stars move in their orbit, their motion shifts features in the system\u2019s spectrum. The shifts reveal a dance that a backyard observer cannot resolve\u2014but can contemplate while looking at the light that reaches us. SIMBAD lists a parallax of 38.50 milliarcseconds; that measurement places the system roughly 85 light-years away. The number is small, but it is the key: as Earth moves around the Sun, the nearby star appears to shift slightly against more distant background stars. Measuring that apparent shift gives astronomers a way to estimate distance.\n\nFor observers, the main challenge is not Ankaa\u2019s brightness but its address. Phoenix lies in the far-southern sky, and Ankaa\u2019s coordinates\u2014about right ascension 00h 26m, declination 42 degrees south\u2014explain why. It is best placed for evening viewing in the months around October and November.\n\nBegin with your unaided eyes, away from bright streetlights, and give them time to adjust to the dark.
